```
sections.text: ## Lech Walesa (b. 1943)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: ### What He Did

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: Walesa was an electrician at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk, Poland. On August 14, 1980, he climbed over the shipyard wall to join a wildcat strike — and through a combination of personal authority, tactical intelligence, and luck became the symbol of a movement that would end communism in Poland.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Gdansk Agreement (August 31, 1980)**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
```
  GDANSK AGREEMENT: WHAT THE WORKERS WON
  ========================================

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
Within 18 days of the strike beginning, the Polish
  communist government signed the Gdansk Agreement:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
1. Right to form independent trade unions (unprecedented
     in Soviet bloc)
  2. Right to strike
  3. Reduction in censorship
  4. Free Saturdays (5-day work week)
  5. Release of political prisoners
  6. Access to mass media for Church and unions

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
SIGNIFICANCE: A communist government had formally recognized
  the right of workers to organize independently of the party.
  This was the first breach in the Soviet model's core assumption:
  that the party represented the workers and independent
  organizations were unnecessary.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
By September 1980: Solidarity has 10 million members.
  Poland's population: 36 million. Total workforce: ~18M.
  More than half the Polish workforce joined within months.
```

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **Martial Law (December 13, 1981)**: General Jaruzelski declared martial law; Solidarity was banned; Walesa was interned for 11 months. He was released in 1982 as a private citizen. The movement continued underground — the Catholic Church provided organizational cover; Western support (CIA, AFL-CIO) provided material.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **Nobel Peace Prize (1983)**: Awarded while Walesa was under government surveillance; he didn't travel to Oslo to accept it (feared he wouldn't be allowed back). His wife Danuta accepted in his place.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Round Table (1989)**: By 1988, the Polish economy was in crisis and the communist government was losing legitimacy. They negotiated with Solidarity — effectively acknowledging that they could not govern without the opposition. The Round Table Agreement (April 1989) allowed partially free elections. Solidarity won 99 of 100 Senate seats (the 1 was their error — they forgot to field a candidate in one constituency). A Solidarity-led government formed — the first non-communist government in the Soviet bloc since the late 1940s.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Post-Communist Walesa**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: Walesa served as Poland's first democratically elected president (1990–95), then was defeated for re-election. His presidency was contentious — autocratic tendencies, theological conservatism (strong Catholic influence on policy), and poor economic management. He was not a good president. His contribution was the movement, not the governance.

sections.text: ## Václav Havel (1936–2011)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: ### Context

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: Havel was a playwright who became dissident who became president. His intellectual contribution — the use of cultural authority as political force — is distinct from any other figure in this directory.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **"The Power of the Powerless" (1978)**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
```
  HAVEL'S ANALYSIS OF COMMUNIST POWER
  ======================================

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
The "greengrocer" thought experiment:
  A greengrocer puts "Workers of the World, Unite!" in his
  window not because he believes it but because everyone does it
  and not doing it would require explanation, courage, conflict.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
The slogan is not a statement of belief.
  It is a participation in a ritual that says:
  "I know the rules. I accept the rules. I am harmless."

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
THE KEY INSIGHT:
  The system doesn't require true believers.
  It requires participation in the ritual.
  Dissent = refusing to participate = exposing the ritual
           = threatening everyone who is participating.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
Hence: dissidents are so threatening even when they have
  no power — they are not a political threat, they are a
  MORAL threat. They expose everyone's complicity.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
THE SOLUTION:
  "Living in truth" — refusing to participate in the ritual.
  This has no immediate political effect.
  Over time, it corrodes the system's legitimacy.
  When the system cracks (for economic or external reasons),
  "living in truth" has prepared the society to act.
```

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **Charter 77 (1977)**: Havel was a primary signatory of Charter 77 — a declaration that demanded the Czechoslovak government respect its own constitution and international human rights agreements it had signed. 241 signatories. The government arrested the leaders, interrogated hundreds, and harassed signatories for years. The Charter was the organizing nucleus of Czechoslovak civil society.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Velvet Revolution (November 1989)**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky
Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

Nov 17: Student demonstration; police beat them brutally
          (false rumor spread that a student had been killed)
  Nov 18: Civic Forum formed (Havel + other dissidents)
  Nov 19: Demonstrations across Prague; 100,000 in Wenceslas Sq.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
MECHANISM: Havel's concept of "living in truth" had
  prepared the moral substrate. When the system cracked
  (Gorbachev signaled no military intervention; economic
  crisis; Polish and Hungarian examples), the accumulated
  refusal to participate collapsed the regime.
```

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Havel Presidency (1989–2003, interrupted by Slovak secession)**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: Havel served as President of Czechoslovakia (1989–92) and then Czech Republic (1993–2003) after the peaceful Velvet Divorce (Slovak and Czech states separated January 1, 1993 — Havel had opposed separation but accepted the democratic decision).

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: His presidency was notable for its moral character and poor political management. He was better as a symbolic figure and conscience than as an executive. He navigated EU and NATO membership processes successfully (both achieved under his successors).

sections.text: ## Mikhail Gorbachev (1931–2022)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: ### The Problem He Faced

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
By 1985, the Soviet Union was in structural decline:
- Oil prices had collapsed (from $40/barrel 1980 to $12/barrel 1986)
- The Afghan War was draining resources and manpower (9 years, 15,000 dead)
- Chernobyl (April 1986) exposed the systemic dysfunction of information suppression
- Computer technology was transforming the global economy; the USSR could not compete
- Consumer goods shortages; corruption endemic; morale collapsed

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: Gorbachev's diagnosis: the system needed to be saved by being opened.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
```
  GORBACHEV'S REFORMS
  ====================

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
GLASNOST ("openness"):
  - Press criticism of government policy permitted
  - Historical crimes (Stalin's terror) acknowledged
  - Chernobyl as the first test: initial suppression,
    then unprecedented disclosure
  - Foreign films, literature; open discussion of
    previously forbidden topics

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
PERESTROIKA ("restructuring"):
  - Economic decentralization: enterprises allowed to
    make some market decisions
  - Cooperatives permitted (small private businesses)
  - Anti-corruption campaigns
  - Reduction of central planning (without replacing it
    with a functioning alternative)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
DEMOCRATIZATION:
  - Congress of People's Deputies (1989): partially free
    elections; televised debates — Soviet citizens watched
    politicians argue in public for the first time
  - Competitive elections within Communist Party
  - Multi-party system (eventually accepted)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
FOREIGN POLICY:
  - Brezhnev Doctrine renounced (1988): Soviet Union will
    not militarily intervene to protect allied governments
  - Afghan withdrawal completed February 1989
  - Arms reduction agreements with Reagan
  - German reunification accepted
```

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Unintended Consequences**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: Glasnost enabled public criticism to escalate faster than controlled reform could proceed. The nationalist movements in the Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania), then Ukraine, Armenia, Georgia, Azerbaijan — all used the new openness to demand independence. Gorbachev didn't intend this. His model was a reformed Soviet Union, not its dissolution.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The August Coup (August 19–21, 1991)**: Communist hardliners placed Gorbachev under house arrest at his Crimean dacha and announced he was ill. Yeltsin climbed on a tank in front of the Russian parliament building and declared the coup illegal. The coup collapsed in three days — the plotters had no plan and no popular support. Gorbachev returned to Moscow to find that Yeltsin, not he, was now the effective power.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **December 1991**: The Soviet Union was formally dissolved. Gorbachev resigned on December 25, 1991.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **Assessment**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
```
  WHAT GORBACHEV INTENDED:    WHAT HAPPENED:
  ========================    ==============

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
Reformed Soviet Union       Soviet Union dissolved
  Marxism with a human face   Capitalism (of various kinds)
  New model for socialism     Yeltsin's oligarchic transition
  Controlled glasnost         Information flood
  Stable transition           Economic collapse, crime wave

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
WAS THIS FAILURE?
  For Gorbachev: yes, catastrophically — he lost his country
  For the world: he ended the Cold War without nuclear war
  For Russia: contested — 1990s were catastrophic
  For Eastern Europe: liberation
  For Germany: reunification

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
Key fact: Gorbachev chose not to use force to hold
  the Soviet bloc together when he could have.
  The Tiananmen comparison is exact: China used force
  in June 1989; the CCP survived. Gorbachev didn't;
  the USSR didn't. His restraint was a political choice.
```

sections.text: ## Aung San Suu Kyi (b. 1945)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: ### Context

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: Suu Kyi's father, Aung San, was the hero of Burmese independence (killed 1947 before independence). She grew up in India and England, married British academic Michael Aris, lived as a scholar. She returned to Burma in 1988 to care for her ill mother — and found herself in the middle of a popular uprising against the military junta.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The 8888 Uprising (August 8, 1988)**: Massive demonstrations against the military regime of Ne Win. Suu Kyi gave her first major speech (August 26, 1988) to 500,000 people. The military (SLORC — State Law and Order Restoration Council) cracked down, killing hundreds. Suu Kyi co-founded the National League for Democracy (NLD).

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **House Arrest (1989–2010)**: The military placed Suu Kyi under house arrest rather than imprisoning her (imprisonment would have been too obviously brutal; house arrest kept her silent while maintaining deniability). She was under house arrest for 15 of the 21 years from 1989 to 2010, with brief periods of freedom.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **Nobel Peace Prize (1991)**: Awarded while she was under house arrest.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Transition (2010–2021)**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: The military began a controlled democratic transition in 2010–11. Suu Kyi was released; the NLD competed in by-elections (2012, winning 43 of 44 seats); competed in general elections (2015, winning 86% of seats); Suu Kyi became State Counsellor (effectively Prime Minister) in 2016.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Rohingya Crisis (2017)**: The military conducted a brutal clearance operation against the Rohingya Muslim minority — killing thousands, raping systematically, burning villages, driving 700,000+ into Bangladesh. Suu Kyi's response: silence, then defense of the military at the International Court of Justice. She argued there was no genocide; the military was responding to terrorist attacks.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
```
  THE COLLAPSE OF THE SAINTLY IMAGE
  ====================================

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
PRE-2017 NARRATIVE:            POST-2017 REALITY:
  ==================             =================
  Democratic icon                Defended ethnic cleansing
  Human rights symbol            at ICJ
  Nobel laureate                 Silence on atrocities
  Prisoner of conscience         Used state power against
                                 journalists (Reuters
                                 reporters jailed 2018)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
EXPLANATION ATTEMPTS:
  1. She was always a Burman nationalist, not a universal
     human rights advocate (religion/ethnicity)
  2. She was protecting a fragile democratic transition
     (can't confront the military or lose everything)
  3. She simply doesn't care about Muslim minorities
  4. She had no actual power over the military

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
The honest answer is probably some combination of all four.
  It does not rehabilitate her conduct.
```

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **Military Coup (February 1, 2021)**: The military annulled the 2020 election results (NLD had won again, massively) and staged a coup. Suu Kyi was arrested, tried on multiple charges (corruption, illegal import of walkie-talkies, COVID rule violations), and sentenced to 27 years in prison. She is reportedly held in solitary confinement.

sections.text: ## Volodymyr Zelensky (b. 1978)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: ### Context

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: Zelensky was a comedian and actor, most famous for playing the President of Ukraine in a TV show ("Servant of the People") — then actually running for president using the show's title as his party name, and winning with 73% of the vote in 2019.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: On February 24, 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **What He Did**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky
Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
Western intelligence had briefed: Kyiv would fall in
  72 hours. Many Western governments were preparing
  evacuation protocols.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
US offer: "I need ammunition, not a ride."
            (Zelensky's response to evacuation offer)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
He stayed. He filmed himself on the street in Kyiv.
  "We are here. We are defending Ukraine."
  This was not military strategy — it was the first
  battle: the information battle, the morale battle,
  the international support battle.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
Within hours: the narrative had shifted from
  "Ukraine is about to fall" to
  "Ukraine is fighting and needs support."

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
This is the exact moment where his background in
  media and performance became a strategic asset.
```

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Communication Strategy**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: Zelensky addressed the UK Parliament, the US Congress, the Bundestag, the Knesset, the Japanese Diet — adapting his rhetoric to each audience's historical memory. Churchill references for the UK. Holocaust references for Germany and Israel. Pearl Harbor for the US. This was sophisticated, calculated political communication.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Political-Military Record (2022–2025)**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
| Year | Military/Political Events |
|------|--------------------------|
| 2022 | Kyiv defense; Russian withdrawal from north; Kharkiv counter-offensive (Sept); Kherson liberation (Nov) |
| 2023 | Bakhmut battle; summer counter-offensive disappoints; mobilization politics |
| 2024 | Kursk incursion (Ukrainian forces into Russia for first time); continuing attrition |
| 2025 | Negotiations pressure; Western support fatigue; holding |

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **Complications**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
Zelensky is not a simple hero narrative. He has:
- Banned opposition parties (including major ones) under wartime emergency
- Cracked down on the Orthodox Church (tied to Moscow)
- Extended his own term without elections (wartime justification; legally contested)
- Navigated the Zaluzhny dismissal (fired the popular general; politically interpreted)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: These are real governance questions in a wartime emergency context. The question is whether these actions are proportionate emergency measures or authoritarian drift — and that question cannot be answered while the war continues.

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Stakes**: Zelensky's specific historical significance is not yet determinable. If Ukraine survives as a democratic state and retains meaningful sovereignty, he is one of the most consequential leaders in modern European history. If the war ends in a settlement that cedes major territory, his significance is more ambiguous. If the state collapses, he is a tragic figure. History is still writing this chapter.

sections.text: ## Mandela Post-Prison (1990–1999)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: (See also 06-CIVIL-RIGHTS.md for the fuller arc)

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: **The Specific Contribution of the 1990s**:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: Mandela's political genius in the transition years was his management of the competing factions:

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky
Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
TENSIONS TO MANAGE:
  - ANC military wing: wanted immediate transfer of power;
    armed struggle not over; punishment of apartheid apparatus
  - White business community: terrified of economic seizure;
    threatening capital flight
  - Right-wing Afrikaners (AWB): threatening armed resistance
  - Inkatha Freedom Party (Zulu): Buthelezi refused to participate
    in ANC framework; political violence in KwaZulu-Natal
  - Communist Party: wanted socialist economic program
  - International community: wanted stability + investment

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text:
MANDELA'S APPROACH:
  - Visited Betsie Verwoerd (widow of apartheid architect)
    at her home in Oranje — gesture of reconciliation over
    the heads of hardliners
  - Wore a Springbok jersey at the 1995 Rugby World Cup —
    the Springbok was the white Afrikaner national symbol;
    the move brought Afrikaners into the new South Africa
  - CODESA negotiations: power-sharing formula for transition
  - Truth and Reconciliation Commission: structured accountability
    rather than prosecution
  - One term: stepped down after 1999; handed to Mbeki
```

metadata.title: Contemporary Reformers: Walesa, Havel, Gorbachev, Suu Kyi, Zelensky

sections.text: The Mandela of the 1990s is the clearest modern example of personal moral authority being deployed as political capital. His 27 years in prison had not embittered him in publicly visible ways — and his visible restraint gave him political leverage that no economic argument or military force could have produced.
